title: Action de Galois sur Teichmüller : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (pages 49-52). Sigma* is the thrice-punctured sphere P^1 - {0,1,inf}. Its punctures are indexed by J (|J| = 3), with the S_3 = G_J symmetry and complex conjugation tau. Sigma~ is the compact bordered surface obtained by replacing each puncture with a boundary circle (a real oriented blow-up). It is a sphere with three holes, homotopy equivalent to Sigma*. Sigma_R is the real circle. Cut at the three punctures, it gives three segments (Dec(Sigma_R, J)) with midpoints Q_i. Their endpoints R_i^omega lie on the boundary circles. underline-omega is the set of orientations / directions. The two hemispheres epsilon, epsilon' have centres P_epsilon, P_epsilon', which are the order-3 symmetry points e^{±i pi/3}. The points S_i^epsilon lie on the boundary circles inside hemisphere epsilon. Page 50 introduced G_J-torsors of simple paths: a (along boundary circles), b (along real segments from Q_i to an endpoint), c (great-circle arcs P_epsilon -> Q_i) and d (great-circle arcs P_epsilon -> S_i^epsilon).

This page: Grothendieck cuts Sigma~ along trees of arcs joining the three holes. This produces five maximal, connected, simply connected open subsets, which will serve as 'thick base points':
(i) Sigma~_epsilon, two of them. Remove the tripod formed by the three d-arcs running from a pole to the three holes. The figure shows that the tripod removed is the one through the opposite pole P_epsilon', with legs s_i^{epsilon'}. So Sigma~_epsilon is essentially hemisphere epsilon thickened, with centre P_epsilon.
(ii) Sigma~_i, three of them. Remove the two closed real segments b_j = supp b_j^omega ∪ supp b_j^omega' for j ≠ i. What remains is everything except two real intervals, with centre Q_i on the remaining real interval.
Simple connectivity: the complement in S^2 consists of the three closed discs plus a connected tree of arcs, hence it is connected. A connected open subset of S^2 with connected complement is simply connected.

He then sets Pi_epsilon = pi_1(Sigma~, Sigma~_epsilon) and Pi_i = pi_1(Sigma~, Sigma~_i). These are fundamental groups with a simply connected subset as base. They are canonically identified with pi_1(Sigma*, Sigma*_epsilon), and hence with pi_1(Sigma*, P_epsilon); similarly Pi_i is identified with pi_1(Sigma*, Q_i). For x in the subset there are canonical 'transitivity isomorphisms' phi_{epsilon,x}: Pi_epsilon -> pi_1(Sigma~, x) and phi_{i,x}: Pi_i -> pi_1(Sigma~, x), given by any path inside the simply connected piece.

Purpose: build a rigid, S_3 x <tau>-equivariant system of base points (two hemispheres plus three real intervals) for the fundamental groupoid of P^1 - {0,1,inf}. On the next page these are linked by the c-paths along the graph with vertices P_epsilon, P_epsilon', Q_i, Q_j, Q_k. Composing around closed cycles gives inner automorphisms. This prepares a combinatorial or Galois-equivariant description of the action on pi_1, the 'epinglage' of pi_1 at all vertices, toward the Galois action on the Teichmüller tower.
errors: The formula Sigma~_epsilon = Sigma~ minus ∪_i supp d_i^epsilon conflicts with the margin figure. The figure has P_epsilon as the centre of Sigma~_epsilon and the removed tripod passing through P_epsilon' with legs s_i^{epsilon'}. Since P_epsilon is declared the centre, the removed arcs should be d_i^{epsilon'}; the formula as written has an epsilon/epsilon' slip.

The page mixes notation for the centres: P_omega / Sigma~_omega in the text versus P_epsilon / Sigma~_epsilon in the formulas, and phi_omega versus phi_epsilon in (29). These are notational inconsistencies, not mathematical ones.
The numbering (27) is reused: page 50 already has a (27) for b~_i^omega.

The phrase 'tous Sigma~' (presumably meaning they are all open in Sigma~ and include boundary points) is elliptic. Simple connectivity holds, but strictly these are open subsets of the bordered surface, not of S^2. The complement argument should be run in S^2 with the three discs adjoined. The argument is correct once read this way.

ideas.what: Using a simply connected (even contractible) subset as a 'base point' for pi_1, with canonical transitivity isomorphisms to pi_1 at each of its points.
ideas.modern_name: Fundamental group based at a simply connected subset; fundamental groupoid on a set of base points
ideas.usually_credited_to: R. Brown (groupoids on several base points, 1967); Deligne 1989 ('Le groupe fondamental de la droite projective moins trois points', simply connected subsets as base points)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) advocates fundamental groupoids based at a suitable Galois-stable set of base points; the explicit construction here is not published

ideas.what: Choosing as base regions the two hemispheres (upper and lower half-planes) and the three real intervals of P^1(R) - {0,1,inf}. The setup is equivariant under S_3 x complex conjugation, and the real intervals are tau-stable.
ideas.modern_name: Real intervals / half-planes as base points; tangential base points; the 'real' Galois-stable base points used in Grothendieck-Teichmüller theory
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ihara, Deligne, Drinfeld (late 1980s-1990); Lochak-Schneps, Nakamura in GT literature
ideas.where_published: Esquisse mentions base points tied to the real structure and the 'Lego'; no explicit five-region construction published

ideas.what: Cutting the pair of pants along trees of arcs joining the boundary components to get maximal simply connected pieces, with 'centres'.
ideas.modern_name: Cut systems / arc systems on a pair of pants (cell decomposition)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical surface topology; Hatcher-Thurston style cut systems

deep.surprise_reason: This is careful bookkeeping in preparation for a combinatorial description of pi_1 of P^1 - {0,1,inf} with symmetric base regions. The idea of base points as simply connected regions (half-planes and real intervals) is standard and appeared independently in Deligne 1989 and in the GT literature. It is of historical interest as an early instance, but nothing here would surprise a specialist.
transcription_corrections: The index set in (27) is J (i ∈ J, j ∈ J∖{i}), not I.
The marginal note in (27) reads 'où b_i = supp b~_i^omega (= supp b_i^omega ∪ supp b_i^omega')', with b, not c. A crossed-out attempt precedes it.
The second line of (27) should read Sigma~_i = Sigma~ minus ∪_{j∈J∖{i}} b_j. The page writes b_i^omega with the 'supp' struck out; the index should be j.
'simplement connexes' carries an insertion 'connexes et 0' (that is, connected with degree of connexion 0). The marginal note reads roughly 'en dehors des … et pour cela voisins connexes…'.

The left margin figure labels are Sigma~_epsilon with P_epsilon, P_epsilon' and legs s_i^{epsilon'}, s_j^{epsilon'}, s_k^{epsilon'}. The second figure shows Sigma~_i with Q_i, Q_j, Q_k, R_i^omega, R_j^omega, R_k^{omega'}.
The page number at the top is '5' (internal numbering), with archive page 51 at the bottom.
